text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson in a weekend speech invited the opposition conservative party, the Moderates, to cooperate with him on law and order issues. He said unemployment would be a key issue in next year's general elections.
- There is no evidence that shows reducing the number of hours of work per week increases employment. Sweden's Gross Domestic Product per capita is lower than that for Europe in general.
- A 19-year-old Swedish vandal must pay about one million crowns in damages, the highest sum ever.

- The fund manager of one of Sweden's largest pension funds, Bo Eklof, manages about 300 billion crowns in insurance company SPP's pension fund which is growing at a record rate. Most of the fund is invested in debt papers but 100 million crowns worth is invested in Swedish and foreign shares. Funds are the main owners of shares on the Stockholm bourse -- only 15 percent of them are owned by individual Swedish investors.

- Several Swedish companies will publish half-year results this week including investment company Investor, drug company Astra, forestry group Stora and appliance maker Electrolux LUXb.ST. More market players are focusing on order intake instead of bottom line result. "People are going to be looking at future development and not so much on the 1997 result," one analyst said. Expectations are quite high for the numbers as the recent sharp rises in stock prices show. Electrolux is expected to show a loss because of costs in the second quarter for the company's large restructuring programme.

- A survey of 190 companies conducted by the newspaper shows that coffers of large Swedish companies are larger than ever before. Despite increased dividends, more research and a number of acquisitions, Sweden's largest companies has now holding over 200 billion crowns in cash.
